pragma solidity >=0.4.22 <0.6;

contract WETH9 {
    string public name     = "Wrapped Ether";
    string public symbol   = "WETH";
    uint8  public decimals = 18;

    event  Approval(address indexed src, address indexed guy, uint wad);
    event  Transfer(address indexed src, address indexed dst, uint wad);
    event  Deposit(address indexed dst, uint wad);
    event  Withdrawal(address indexed src, uint wad);

    mapping (address => uint)                       public  balanceOf;
    mapping (address => mapping (address => uint))  public  allowance;

    function() external payable {
        deposit();
    }
    function deposit() public payable {
        balanceOf[msg.sender] += msg.value;
        emit Deposit(msg.sender, msg.value);
    }
    function withdraw(uint wad) public {
        require(balanceOf[msg.sender] >= wad);
        balanceOf[msg.sender] -= wad;
        msg.sender.transfer(wad);
        emit Withdrawal(msg.sender, wad);
    }

    function totalSupply() public view returns (uint) {
        return address(this).balance;
    }

    function approve(address guy, uint wad) public returns (bool) {
        allowance[msg.sender][guy] = wad;
        emit Approval(msg.sender, guy, wad);
        return true;
    }

    function transfer(address dst, uint wad) public returns (bool) {
        return transferFrom(msg.sender, dst, wad);
    }

    function transferFrom(address src, address dst, uint wad)
        public
        returns (bool)
    {
        require(balanceOf[src] >= wad);

        if (src != msg.sender && allowance[src][msg.sender] != uint(-1)) {
            require(allowance[src][msg.sender] >= wad);
            allowance[src][msg.sender] -= wad;
        }

        balanceOf[src] -= wad;
        balanceOf[dst] += wad;

        emit Transfer(src, dst, wad);

        return true;
    }
}

contracts.name: WETH9

health.headline: Nothing critical, and 4 medium severity issues worth a look.

contracts.purpose: WETH9 wraps native Ether into an ERC-20-style token at a 1:1 ratio. Users deposit ETH to receive balance credit, move it with standard transfer/approve/transferFrom semantics, and withdraw it to get ETH back.

threats.title: Drain contract balance through reentrancy
threats.target: Invariant: Withdraw reduces the caller's balance by wad and sends exactly wad ETH to the caller.
threats.approach: An attacker could exploit the withdraw function by re-entering it during the ETH transfer, allowing them to withdraw more ETH than their balance before it is decremented.

threats.title: Manipulate allowance for unauthorized transfers
threats.target: Asset: allowance mapping; Invariant: When src is not msg.sender and the allowance is not the max uint, the allowance must be at least wad and is reduced by wad.
threats.approach: An attacker could approve an unlimited allowance to a malicious contract and then use transferFrom to drain the owner's tokens without their consent, as the allowance is not decremented for unlimited approvals.

threats.title: Inconsistent totalSupply due to failed withdrawals
threats.target: Invariant: totalSupply equals the contract's ETH balance, which should be at least the sum of all balanceOf entries.
threats.approach: If an attacker causes a withdrawal to fail (e.g., by manipulating gas limits), the totalSupply may not reflect the actual ETH balance, leading to inconsistencies in the contract's state.

threats.title: Exploit fallback function for unauthorized deposits
threats.target: Asset: Native ETH held by the contract's own balance.
threats.approach: An attacker could send ETH to the fallback function without proper checks, potentially leading to unexpected state changes or deposits that are not accounted for correctly.

threats.title: Overwriting allowances without user consent
threats.target: Invariant: approve overwrites the allowance for (msg.sender, guy) with the given value.
threats.approach: An attacker could trick a user into calling approve with a malicious contract address, allowing the attacker to overwrite the user's allowance and gain unauthorized access to their tokens.

findings.description: 5 slots across 3 pages. Monad pays 8,100 gas for the first touch of each 128-slot page, so slots that sit alone on a page cost more than they would on a per-slot schedule. Summed over the 3 calls traced, that is +7,900 gas. Affects monad. Storage delta: +7,900 gas.

findings.title: How long before your app can say the transaction is done
findings.description: Monad reaches deterministic finality in 600 ms, two consensus slots. Base and Arbitrum One confirm through a single sequencer within a couple of seconds, but that confirmation is a promise from the operator; irreversible settlement waits on Ethereum, and a withdrawal waits seven days. Ethereum itself takes about 12.8 minutes. Which number matters depends on what the user is allowed to do next. Affects base, arbitrum. Monad hard finality: 600 ms.

findings.title: Rollups charge for calldata on top of execution gas
findings.description: Base, Arbitrum One publish every transaction's calldata to Ethereum and bill for it separately, and the figures here are execution gas only. The traced calls carry a median of 36 bytes each. Measured against those chains' own fee oracles the omitted charge is fractions of a cent even for a 39 KB deployment, since EIP-4844 blobs made data posting nearly free, so it is a real gap rather than a large one. It moves with Ethereum's fee market, not with your contract. Affects base, arbitrum. Median calldata: 36 B.

findings.title: Monad has no global mempool
findings.description: Transactions are forwarded to the next few block leaders rather than gossiped network-wide, so anything that watches pending transactions works differently. This contract does not appear to depend on pending-transaction visibility, so it is context rather than a change. Affects monad.

findings.fix: This is an accepted trade-off of WETH9, which is deliberately immutable. For new code, send ETH with a low-level call and rely on the existing decrement-before-send ordering or a reentrancy guard. Otherwise document that contract integrators should transfer WETH to an EOA or use a wrapper.
findings.title: withdraw uses transfer with a 2300 gas stipend, so contract wallets with non-trivial receive logic cannot withdraw
findings.description:
No funds are lost, but WETH held by affected contracts cannot be unwrapped by calling withdraw from them. It can be moved to an EOA with transfer and unwrapped there. Contracts that integrate WETH and need the ETH back can get stuck.

What the attacker gets: An attacker gains nothing. The cost falls on contract holders, who must route around the limit.

What has to be true first: The holder is a contract whose receive path costs more than 2300 gas, which is common for proxy wallets. Contracts deployed to this code later may also be affected by gas repricing.

How it is exploited:
1. A contract wallet, such as a multisig or proxy wallet, whose receive or fallback logic needs more than 2300 gas holds WETH. 2. It calls withdraw (line 38). The balance is decremented at line 40, then msg.sender.transfer(wad) at line 41 forwards only 2300 gas. 3. The receiving fallback runs out of gas, the transfer reverts, and the whole call reverts with it. 4. The holder cannot unwrap directly from that contract. This is not attacker-driven. It is a liveness limitation, and a gas repricing hard fork can change which contracts it affects.

findings.fix: No change is needed to the contract, since the invariant holds as 'at least the sum of balances'. Integrators should not rely on strict equality.
findings.title: totalSupply is read from the ETH balance, so forced ETH makes it exceed the sum of balances
findings.description:
Integrators that assume the sum of balances equals totalSupply, or that infer a balance from it, may break. The ETH is stranded in the contract. The sender cannot recover it and no holder is harmed.

What the attacker gets: The attacker gains nothing, and the forced ETH is lost to them. It is a griefing vector only.

What has to be true first: Only the capacity to force-send ETH. Any integration that depends on totalSupply equalling the sum of balances is affected.

How it is exploited:
1. An attacker sends ETH to the contract via selfdestruct or a coinbase payout, which bypasses the fallback at line 31. 2. address(this).balance rises while no balanceOf entry changes. 3. totalSupply at line 46 now overstates the sum of token balances.

chains.name: Monad
caveats: Gas is charged on the transaction's gas limit, not the gas it uses, so a padded limit is money spent.
Cold account access costs 10,100 gas against 2,600 elsewhere, which makes call-heavy contracts use more gas units.
There is no global mempool. Transactions are forwarded to the next few leaders instead.
EIP-4844 blob transactions are not supported.
Full nodes do not serve arbitrary historical state, so some indexing patterns need an archive provider.
EIP-7702 delegated accounts cannot be taken below 10 MON and cannot use CREATE or CREATE2.
The ecosystem is younger than the established L2s, so fewer battle-tested integrations exist.

chains.name: Ethereum
caveats: The most expensive execution environment of the group by a wide margin.
Two epochs, roughly 12.8 minutes, before a block is economically final.
24 KB contract size limit forces large systems into proxies or diamonds.

chains.name: Base
caveats: A single sequencer orders every transaction, so liveness depends on one operator.
Each transaction pays an L1 data fee on top of execution gas, which dominates for calldata-heavy calls.
Withdrawals to Ethereum sit behind a seven-day challenge window.
Execution is sequential, so a parallel-friendly contract layout buys nothing.

chains.name: Arbitrum One
caveats: `block.number` returns an L1 block number, which breaks contracts that assume L2 block cadence.
Transactions pay an L1 data component that is often larger than execution gas.
A single sequencer orders every transaction.
Withdrawals to Ethereum sit behind a seven-day challenge window.
Execution is sequential, so a parallel-friendly contract layout buys nothing.

chains.name: Polygon PoS
caveats: Security comes from its own validator set rather than from Ethereum.
Execution is sequential, so a parallel-friendly contract layout buys nothing.
Historically prone to reorgs of several blocks under load.

chains.name: BNB Smart Chain
caveats: A small validator set relative to Ethereum.
Execution is sequential, so a parallel-friendly contract layout buys nothing.

Gas figures come from executing the contract in a local EVM with synthesised arguments. A function guarded by a balance or permission check will revert, and reverted calls are marked rather than counted.
Only state-changing functions are traced. View and pure functions cost nothing to call from outside a transaction.

Only execution and intrinsic gas is modelled. Rollups additionally charge for publishing calldata to Ethereum, which is not included. Measured against the live oracles, that fee is around $0.0001 on Base and $0.00002 on Arbitrum even for a 39 KB deployment, three to four orders of magnitude below the execution cost shown, because EIP-4844 blobs made data posting nearly free.
Ethereum storage cost is measured from the EVM. The Monad figure is that measurement adjusted by the published MIP-8 schedule.

pragma solidity >=0.4.22 <0.6;

contract WETH9 {
    string public name     = "Wrapped Ether";
    string public symbol   = "WETH";
    uint8  public decimals = 18;

    event  Approval(address indexed src, address indexed guy, uint wad);
    event  Transfer(address indexed src, address indexed dst, uint wad);
    event  Deposit(address indexed dst, uint wad);
    event  Withdrawal(address indexed src, uint wad);

    mapping (address => uint)                       public  balanceOf;
    mapping (address => mapping (address => uint))  public  allowance;

    function() external payable {
        deposit();
    }
    function deposit() public payable {
        balanceOf[msg.sender] += msg.value;
        emit Deposit(msg.sender, msg.value);
    }
    function withdraw(uint wad) public {
        require(balanceOf[msg.sender] >= wad);
        balanceOf[msg.sender] -= wad;
        msg.sender.transfer(wad);
        emit Withdrawal(msg.sender, wad);
    }

    function totalSupply() public view returns (uint) {
        return address(this).balance;
    }

    function approve(address guy, uint wad) public returns (bool) {
        allowance[msg.sender][guy] = wad;
        emit Approval(msg.sender, guy, wad);
        return true;
    }

    function transfer(address dst, uint wad) public returns (bool) {
        return transferFrom(msg.sender, dst, wad);
    }

    function transferFrom(address src, address dst, uint wad)
        public
        returns (bool)
    {
        require(balanceOf[src] >= wad);

        if (src != msg.sender && allowance[src][msg.sender] != uint(-1)) {
            require(allowance[src][msg.sender] >= wad);
            allowance[src][msg.sender] -= wad;
        }

        balanceOf[src] -= wad;
        balanceOf[dst] += wad;

        emit Transfer(src, dst, wad);

        return true;
    }
}

pragma solidity >=0.4.22 <0.6;

contract WETH9 {
    string public constant name     = "Wrapped Ether";
    string public constant symbol   = "WETH";
    uint8  public constant decimals = 18;

    event  Approval(address indexed src, address indexed guy, uint wad);
    event  Transfer(address indexed src, address indexed dst, uint wad);
    event  Deposit(address indexed dst, uint wad);
    event  Withdrawal(address indexed src, uint wad);

    mapping (address => uint)                       public  balanceOf;
    mapping (address => mapping (address => uint))  public  allowance;

    function() external payable {
        deposit();
    }
    function deposit() public payable {
        balanceOf[msg.sender] += msg.value;
        emit Deposit(msg.sender, msg.value);
    }
    function withdraw(uint wad) public {
        require(balanceOf[msg.sender] >= wad);
        balanceOf[msg.sender] -= wad;
        msg.sender.transfer(wad);
        emit Withdrawal(msg.sender, wad);
    }

    function totalSupply() public view returns (uint) {
        return address(this).balance;
    }

    function approve(address guy, uint wad) public returns (bool) {
        allowance[msg.sender][guy] = wad;
        emit Approval(msg.sender, guy, wad);
        return true;
    }

    function transfer(address dst, uint wad) public returns (bool) {
        return transferFrom(msg.sender, dst, wad);
    }

    function transferFrom(address src, address dst, uint wad)
        public
        returns (bool)
    {
        require(balanceOf[src] >= wad);

        if (src != msg.sender && allowance[src][msg.sender] != uint(-1)) {
            require(allowance[src][msg.sender] >= wad);
            allowance[src][msg.sender] -= wad;
        }

        balanceOf[src] -= wad;
        balanceOf[dst] += wad;

        emit Transfer(src, dst, wad);

        return true;
    }
}

changes.why: They never change, so storing them costs three storage slots at deploy and a storage read on every lookup. As constants they live in the bytecode. The getters callers use are unchanged.

health.headline: Nothing critical, and 4 medium severity issues worth a look.

findings.title: No Constructor Defined
findings.description: Contract has no constructor for initialization
findings.fix: Add constructor if initial setup is needed

findings.title: Storage contention on allowance
findings.description: Addressed by a runtime key. withdraw, approve, transfer and transferFrom only serialise against another transaction that uses the same key. Written by withdraw, approve, transfer, transferFrom.
findings.fix: Narrow the addressing of allowance so two transactions only meet when they mean to.

findings.title: Storage contention on balanceOf
findings.description: Addressed by a runtime key. deposit, withdraw, transfer and transferFrom only serialise against another transaction that uses the same key. Written by deposit, withdraw, transfer, transferFrom.

findings.title: withdraw uses transfer with a 2300 gas stipend, so contract wallets with non-trivial receive logic cannot withdraw
findings.description:
No funds are lost, but WETH held by affected contracts cannot be unwrapped by calling withdraw from them. It can be moved to an EOA with transfer and unwrapped there. Contracts that integrate WETH and need the ETH back can get stuck.

What the attacker gets: An attacker gains nothing. The cost falls on contract holders, who must route around the limit.

What has to be true first: The holder is a contract whose receive path costs more than 2300 gas, which is common for proxy wallets. Contracts deployed to this code later may also be affected by gas repricing.

How it is exploited:
1. A contract wallet, such as a multisig or proxy wallet, whose receive or fallback logic needs more than 2300 gas holds WETH. 2. It calls withdraw (line 38). The balance is decremented at line 40, then msg.sender.transfer(wad) at line 41 forwards only 2300 gas. 3. The receiving fallback runs out of gas, the transfer reverts, and the whole call reverts with it. 4. The holder cannot unwrap directly from that contract. This is not attacker-driven. It is a liveness limitation, and a gas repricing hard fork can change which contracts it affects.
findings.fix: This is an accepted trade-off of WETH9, which is deliberately immutable. For new code, send ETH with a low-level call and rely on the existing decrement-before-send ordering or a reentrancy guard. Otherwise document that contract integrators should transfer WETH to an EOA or use a wrapper.

findings.title: totalSupply is read from the ETH balance, so forced ETH makes it exceed the sum of balances
findings.description:
Integrators that assume the sum of balances equals totalSupply, or that infer a balance from it, may break. The ETH is stranded in the contract. The sender cannot recover it and no holder is harmed.

What the attacker gets: The attacker gains nothing, and the forced ETH is lost to them. It is a griefing vector only.

What has to be true first: Only the capacity to force-send ETH. Any integration that depends on totalSupply equalling the sum of balances is affected.

How it is exploited:
1. An attacker sends ETH to the contract via selfdestruct or a coinbase payout, which bypasses the fallback at line 31. 2. address(this).balance rises while no balanceOf entry changes. 3. totalSupply at line 46 now overstates the sum of token balances.
findings.fix: No change is needed to the contract, since the invariant holds as 'at least the sum of balances'. Integrators should not rely on strict equality.

chains.name: Monad
caveats: Gas is charged on the transaction's gas limit, not the gas it uses, so a padded limit is money spent.
Cold account access costs 10,100 gas against 2,600 elsewhere, which makes call-heavy contracts use more gas units.
There is no global mempool. Transactions are forwarded to the next few leaders instead.
EIP-4844 blob transactions are not supported.
Full nodes do not serve arbitrary historical state, so some indexing patterns need an archive provider.
EIP-7702 delegated accounts cannot be taken below 10 MON and cannot use CREATE or CREATE2.
The ecosystem is younger than the established L2s, so fewer battle-tested integrations exist.

chains.name: Ethereum
caveats: The most expensive execution environment of the group by a wide margin.
Two epochs, roughly 12.8 minutes, before a block is economically final.
24 KB contract size limit forces large systems into proxies or diamonds.

chains.name: Base
caveats: A single sequencer orders every transaction, so liveness depends on one operator.
Each transaction pays an L1 data fee on top of execution gas, which dominates for calldata-heavy calls.
Withdrawals to Ethereum sit behind a seven-day challenge window.
Execution is sequential, so a parallel-friendly contract layout buys nothing.

chains.name: Arbitrum One
caveats: `block.number` returns an L1 block number, which breaks contracts that assume L2 block cadence.
Transactions pay an L1 data component that is often larger than execution gas.
A single sequencer orders every transaction.
Withdrawals to Ethereum sit behind a seven-day challenge window.
Execution is sequential, so a parallel-friendly contract layout buys nothing.

chains.name: Polygon PoS
caveats: Security comes from its own validator set rather than from Ethereum.
Execution is sequential, so a parallel-friendly contract layout buys nothing.
Historically prone to reorgs of several blocks under load.

chains.name: BNB Smart Chain
caveats: A small validator set relative to Ethereum.
Execution is sequential, so a parallel-friendly contract layout buys nothing.
